title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
gist: Oregon State University researchers found smoke-tainted hops cause smoky, medicinal off-flavors when used for dry-hopping but are indistinguishable when added during wort boiling, and recommend keeping tainted hops below 50% of dry-hop blends to limit wildfire losses for a Pacific Northwest region that grows over 95% of US hops.

insights.claim: The Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, so wildfire smoke taint there carries significant economic risk for beer brewing.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Hop supply is geographically concentrated; regional wildfires are a supply/quality risk for brewers.

insights.claim: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, killed 11 people, and produced smoke taint that damaged both local wine production and hops grown for brewing.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Climate-driven wildfire events create agricultural quality losses beyond direct burn damage.

insights.claim: Smoke taint in hops is caused mainly by volatile phenols, produced when lignin in plant cells is exposed to wildfire heat; smoke exposure during hop drying increased phenol uptake and gave hops meaty, smoky, artificial BBQ and medicinal notes that overpower citrus aromas.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism of crop quality loss and why post-harvest drying conditions matter.

insights.claim: Oregon State University's Thomas Shellhammer and Cade Jobe found that beers dry-hopped with smoke-tainted Cascade hops had volatile phenol concentrations and smoky/medicinal flavors that rose with the share of tainted hops used.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Dose-dependent taint means blending ratios can control quality outcomes.

insights.claim: When smoke-tainted hops were added during wort boiling rather than dry-hopping, blind tasters could not distinguish the beer from untainted beer, even though volatile phenol concentrations still rose.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Brewers can route tainted hop lots to boil additions, salvaging value from damaged crops.

insights.claim: Researchers recommend brewers keep smoke-tainted hops below 50 percent of the blend when dry-hopping, allowing tainted batches to be used and reducing wildfire's economic impact on beer production.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Practical guideline that can reduce write-offs for hop growers after smoke events.

insights.claim: The OSU hop-taint findings may not extend to wine, because fermentation processes differ and grapes make up almost all of wine's raw material while hops are a small fraction of beer ingredients.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Wine producers remain more exposed to smoke taint than brewers.

insights.claim: Further work is needed to confirm the hop blending ratios, test hops smoke-exposed in the field while still metabolically active, and run consumer acceptance studies of blended-hop beers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Guidance is preliminary; don't overstate mitigation until replicated.

insights.claim: Hops contain starch enzymes that can trigger excessive re-fermentation after bottling ('hop creep'), so dry-hopped beers produce much higher CO2 and package pressures, which Shellhammer identified in 2018 as the likely cause of exploding beer bottles.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Dry-hopping popularity among craft brewers carries packaging-safety and quality-control costs.
